content: 1. For every 10,000 liters of liquid formulations, at least one sample must be tested. 2. For solid formulations, a minimum of one sample per batch must be tested. If the batch size exceeds 5,000 kg, at least one sample should be tested for every 5,000 kg. 3. For long-lasting insecticidal nets (LNs), the buyer or procurement entity must determine the number, frequency, and distribution of nets to be tested within and between batches and consignments, balancing cost and risk. 4. Sampling frequency based on probability is outlined in Annex 4. Sampling of LNs can also follow ISO 2859 standards for inspection by attributes. 5. Immediately after a sample is collected, it must be identified in the inspector’s handwriting with a unique reference number, date, and initials. It should then be officially sealed and recorded. 6. The sampling report (Annex 3) and chain-of-custody record (Annex 5) must be completed and signed by both the party providing the sample and the inspector. 7. The first subsample should be given to the party from whom the sample was taken, allowing them to send it to a laboratory for analysis if they question the test results. 8. The second subsample must be sent by the inspector to the designated laboratory within one week, accompanied by a form requesting analysis (Annex 6). The analyst must sign the chain-of-custody record. 9. The analyst should be given a deadline to complete the analysis, typically within 4 weeks for fresh samples or 6 weeks for tests involving accelerated storage (e.g., 8 weeks at 40°C). 10. The third subsample should be retained by the procurement entity as a backup in case of disputes regarding the results of the first two subsamples. 11. During packaging and transport, care must be taken to prevent spillage, leakage, or deterioration of samples. Improperly packed pesticide samples that break during transport can pose health risks to handlers and laboratory staff. 12. Each sealed sample container must be placed in a plastic bag, sealed with tape, and secured in a larger container lined with absorbent material to immobilize the sample bottles and absorb any leakage. 13. Sampling reports should be placed in a separate sealed plastic bag within the container. The container should then be filled with additional absorbent material, closed, and sealed. 14. Labels must be securely attached to the container, indicating the shipper’s name and address, the testing laboratory’s address and contact information, the appropriate hazard classification of the pesticide, and arrows indicating the up position of the samples. 15. Samples must be accompanied by a material safety data sheet (if available), a declaration of dangerous goods, and a non-commercial proforma invoice for customs clearance, as applicable. 16. When transporting pesticide samples, regulations from the International Civil Aviation Organization, International Maritime Organization, and other relevant bodies must be followed to ensure safe handling and compliance. 17. Independent quality control analysis should be conducted by a certified or accredited laboratory to verify compliance with WHO or other relevant specifications. 18. A contract must be established between the laboratory and the requesting party, specifying all relevant details for quality control, including test methods, confidentiality clauses, costs, and archiving of raw data and samples. 19. The analysis should include not only the active ingredient content but also all physical and chemical properties specified in the WHO or other relevant specifications. 20. The laboratory must provide a comprehensive report of the analysis, including details such as the number of samples, trade name, declared active ingredient content, supplier, manufacturer, batch number, receipt date, storage conditions, and test results. 21. The report should summarize results, conclusions on compliance, and any additional information to facilitate interpretation. It must be signed by the responsible analyst or laboratory manager and sent to the requesting party. 22. National regulations for procurement typically include provisions for penalizing noncompliance with tender conditions. Bidders submitting incomplete, false, or misleading offers should be disqualified, and legal action may be taken depending on the severity of the offense. 23. Customs clearance for pesticide imports requires close collaboration between the pesticide regulatory authority and customs offices. Advance notice of shipment arrivals is often necessary. 24. Emergency procurement provisions should allow for the importation of unregistered public health pesticides under specified conditions with the competent authority’s permission. 25. Traceability systems must be in place to record the distribution of procured pesticides, ensuring they can be traced to local warehouses and recalled if found noncompliant. 26. WHO specifications define minimum acceptable criteria for good-quality products, and samples must be tested for compliance with all specified clauses and limits. 27. Omission of expensive or time-consuming tests from quality control increases the risk of accepting poor-quality products and is not recommended. In exceptional cases, such as emergencies, some tests may be omitted with mutual agreement. 28. The Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) promotes international agreement on pesticide analysis methods and provides widely recognized methods for testing compliance with physical and chemical properties. WHO specifications recommend using CIPAC methods for pesticide quality control.
